items.title: Node and relay split: the review of 2026-10-10
items.box:
WHAT: act on the review "SpiritOS relay and node split review" (Andreas Thut, 2026-10-10, at e8f8ffd; relay.js whole and the node's wire path read by four readers; S1, S3, S6 reproduced on Node 22). Its verdict: the relay keeps its envelope rule, the node breaks its own, both layers still carry app knowledge, and the worst problems are trust, not layering. The rules checked are NODE-AND-RELAY.md's three: the relay carries, the node stores, the shell understands.

DECIDED: the goal is Andy's (2026-10-10); "device WILL be KILLED. that's a decision." (2026-10-10, under goal/G16.2: the device enrolment, abandoned 2026-09-26, leaves the tree, as an item of this goal once he adds it); "the relays should do first-claim, it should happen at install time. that's the only \"safe\" way." and "NOT first claim i mean" and "KILL the dead code / fallback. this type of stuff is always coming back to bite us." BYTES must be counted. that's a rule." (2026-10-10, under goal/G16.6; it covers R5 as well); items are added one at a time at his word; every relay-wire and node-verb change is reviewed and gets his yes before a build. Claude-windows checked the headline items in the tree at b355e36d; the low items stand on the review's word until their item opens.

items.title: Bodies read as Buffers and joined once (R1)
items.box:
WHAT: every HTTP body the node or the relay reads off a socket is collected as Buffers and decoded once at the end, so a multi-byte character split across two TCP chunks arrives whole; today each chunk is turned into a string on its own and the split character becomes U+FFFD, a request then fails its signature with a spurious 403, and a reply, which no signature covers until goal/G16.1, arrives changed and nobody notices (R1 of the review).

DECIDED: this item at Andy's word (2026-10-10, "Q6: Add it? yes"). On the studio call (2026-10-10): "on the wire to unsloth studio, all is permitted, deskUnsloth is responsible to keep the request bodies to desk, and the streams to \"owner\" and UI within packet limits." So that reach needs no exemption and no tally entry; deskUnsloth owns what it sends on and keeps it under the packet caps. The four readers were discussed one at a time ("THIS IS NOT A ONE-ANSWER"); his rulings, 2026-10-10: "4. yes. the relayRequest must copy raw bytes only. if it doesn't fix it. now."; "3. serveCommon. yes. one single piece of shared code must ensure that raw bytes are copied. precisely."; "2. same practise odered. ideally through a shared kernel.js utility or similar."; "1. already decided and defined". The rule behind it, his, 2026-10-10: "in a max_BYTE environment, BYTES must be copied. BYTES must be counted. that's a rule." R5 folded in on that rule: "yes. just make sure it's fixed." (2026-10-10).

CHECKED by claude-windows at b355e36d:
- relayRequest.js 80: the node's one hop to a relay collects the answer with chunks += c (a string from the start) and resolves text: chunks. Every relay answer the node reads passes here.
- serveCommon.js 173: readJsonBody, the body reader of node and relay alike, does body += chunk after counting Buffer.byteLength(chunk) against the cap (the cap counts bytes correctly; the join does not).
- kernel.js 625: the node-side fetch in the kernel does data += chunk the same way; deskUnsloth.js 214 (the studio call) raw += c as well. The desk's own readers go through appServer, not read here.
- Node's Buffer.concat(chunks).toString('utf8') decodes once over the whole body and never splits a character; a chunk is a Buffer when no encoding is set on the stream, so the fix is in the join, not the stream.

SHAPE (decided)
1. ONE SHARED UTILITY in kernel.js, the file node and processes both load: readBody(stream) collects the raw chunks as Buffers and decodes once at the end, Buffer.concat(list).toString('utf8'), answering a promise of the text; it takes an optional byte cap and refuses by name when the raw bytes pass it, counting Buffer.byteLength per chunk before the push, so readJsonBody keeps its cap exactly as today.
2. THREE READERS USE IT and keep no reading of their own: relayRequest (the outbound socket, node and relay), serveCommon.readJsonBody (the one door's body reader, node and relay), and the kernel's own jobs.report (a process reading its node's answer). The studio call in deskUnsloth is off this item (his ruling 1).
3. BYTES COUNTED (R5, folded): the relay's four size checks that compare text.length against MAX_ROUTED_TEXT (relay.js 2701, 4063, 4181, 4250) compare Buffer.byteLength(text, 'utf8') instead, so a non-ASCII text is refused at the cap it names and not at the HTTP body cap.
4. Nothing on the wire changes; oneDoor's tally does not move (no new require of http anywhere).

TESTS, red first: spirit/test/bodiesJoinedOnce.js: kernel exports readBody and a body whose four-byte character (an emoji) is split across two writes with a pause between them comes back exact (red today: no such utility); relayRequest resolves the exact text of such an answer from a local server (red today: U+FFFD in it); readJsonBody of serveCommon parses the exact string of such a request and still refuses a body one byte over its cap; jobs.report hands back such an answer whole; the three files hold no chunk-to-string join of their own (the grep for the idiom under them is empty); a routed text whose byte count passes MAX_ROUTED_TEXT while its character count does not (accents or emoji) is refused 413 too big by the relay, and relay.js compares no text length against that cap any more.

FILES: kernel.js, relayRequest.js, serveCommon.js, relay.js (core, grant); spirit/test/bodiesJoinedOnce.js (new).

FOLDED IN (Andy, 2026-10-10: "place all you can into existing items, then we deal with the rest."):
- S10: relayRequest has no socket timeout, no response size cap and no error handler, so a partner or a relay can stream an endless body into RAM or hold sockets open; the shared readBody takes the cap and relayRequest sets a timeout and an error handler, refusing by name.
- The proxy's reply (his net.fetch question under the goal): handleGenericProxy reads an outside reply whole with no cap; it reads through the same readBody with a cap and refuses by name past it.
- Low: the carry branch runs before the text type and size checks (relay.js 4126 vs 4178); the checks come first.

RULED ON THE BUILD (Andy, 2026-10-11): on the relay answer, "and answer from a relay is ALWAYS bounded by MAX_PAYLOAD. how the hell could it be otherwise?" and "no shell bundle ever comes through relays.": relayRequest refuses an answer above limits.BODY_MAX by name, no figure of its own. On the proxy reply, "agreed. no number at all.": the proxy passes the outside reply straight through to the asker as it arrives, unread and undecoded, so it holds nothing and needs no limit (his 2026-09-22 words, "size limits would break the proxy facility real quick", stand).

why is there a relayRequest, isn't that just another peerRequest?

relayRequest is not another interface; it is the socket under the one interface. peerPost is the signed request (hash, signature, dispatch by hash) and it rides on relayRequest for the outbound half, which is the one place in the node layer that requires http at all; the relay itself is handed the same function for its partner calls, and the oneDoor tally counts it like every other file.
Its direct callers besides peerPost are the relay's own public doors that are not posts to a peer, because they name no target key: fetching a relay's key, the claim, and the badge's who-probe, all from hub.
That socket is also what the review's S10 names (no timeout, no size cap, no error handler), which is why the byte-joining fix of this item lands in it; the yes-or-no above still stands.
are you asking if a relay should reject a request immediately with error if it has no known signature?

No. This item is only about how a body is read off a socket: four readers glue chunks together as text and can break a character in half; the fix is to collect the raw chunks and decode once. The review named two readers; two more read the same way, the process report in the kernel and deskUnsloth's studio call.
A relay does refuse a request whose signature is unknown or wrong, before anything else; what the review found there is that it counts the request against the claimed sender's rate limit before checking the signature (S4), which is the next batch, not this item.
So, plainly: apply the same fix to those two extra readers in this item, yes or no?

which four reader glue chunks together, and why does each one do it. 

bulleted list please.

The four, and what each reads:
- relayRequest (node, and the relay for its partner calls): reads a relay's answer to every post, claim, key fetch and probe; it is the one outbound socket.
- readJsonBody in serveCommon (node and relay): reads the body of every HTTP request that arrives at the one door.
- the process report in the kernel: a spawned process reads its own node's answer when it reports a job update.
- the studio call in deskUnsloth: reads the model studio's answer to a chat or model request.
Why each glues: all four were written with the usual idiom, add each chunk to a string as it arrives, which turns every chunk into text on its own; a character split across two chunks then becomes two broken halves. None has a reason to read that way; collecting the raw chunks and decoding once is the same length of code.

- the studio call in deskUnsloth: on the wire to unsloth studio, all is permitted, deskUnsloth is responsible to keep the request bodies to desk, and the streams to "owner" and UI within packet limits.

- the process report: What's wrong with that? Where does it concatenate?

- what is serveCommon, and why/where does it concatenate?

- relayRequest: why should relayRequest, read contents of bodies? I thought it shouldn't/couldn't.....


i need to discuss each of those things separately. THIS IS NOT A ONE-ANSWER do me.

1. The studio call: your ruling is in the box, all is permitted on that wire and deskUnsloth keeps what it sends on under the packet caps; so no exemption and no tally entry for it, and its reading is deskUnsloth's own business. Taken off this item.

2. The process report: in the kernel, spirit.core.jobs.report is what a spawned process calls to send a job update to its own node through the one door; it reads the node's answer with the add-each-chunk idiom (kernel line 625). Nothing is wrong with it in practice: the answer is a few bytes of plain JSON from its own node, so a split character cannot occur unless the node ever echoes non-ASCII text in that answer. It was on my list for sameness, not for a fault; I propose leaving it out.

3. serveCommon: the small module both servers share for answering HTTP, since the node and the relay became separate programs (cycle 0): reading a request body, sending a file, refusing a body that is too big or malformed, saying which build runs. items.title: Receipt binds the reply text; forwarded reply verified (S1, S2)
items.box:
WHAT: the receipt a node signs for its reply also binds the reply's text, so neither relay on the path nor a partner can swap the text under a receipt that still verifies (S1); and a relay verifies a forwarded reply's receipt before it announces the route that reply proves (S2). Both from the review of 2026-10-10 (repro of S1: "receipt verifies with forged text: true").

DECIDED (Andy, 2026-10-10): the goal ("Greate a goal in desk for this"); this item ("Q1: Add it? yes."). A relay-wire change: the shape is reviewed and gets his yes before any build. On Q1: "flag day. we don't maintain backward compatibility before alpha, maybe not even before beta, the data stored in the SpiritOS is never in danger." Checked: the only stored receipts are traffic-log rows, read back for the replay index by hash and time and never re-verified (the two verifiers run on arrival only), so nothing stored is touched. CHECKED by claude-windows at b355e36d:
- relayAuth.js receiptMessage(hash, atMs) is 'receipt', the REQUEST hash and the minute; receiptSignatureOk tries minutes -1, 0, +1. Nothing names the reply text.
- Producers: peerPost.js 1058 and 1084 (card asks), 1483 (the answer to an arrival, bare or with text); relay.js 2976 (relayErrorToAsker, the relay speaking as itself) and 3219 (the device offer).
- Verifiers: peerPost.js onReply 1565 (the asker); relay.js routeReply 4256 (the member's own relay, before routes.answer). deliverForwardedReply (relay.js 2980) verifies nothing: routes.answer by from, announceRoute, send; its comment says the bar is the signed reply.
- The seal is anonymous ephemeral-static (seal.js): anybody holding the asker's seal key can seal text "from" the target, so only the receipt can bind the text.

1. receiptMessage(hash, text, atMs): 'receipt', the request hash, the sha256 of the reply text (the empty text hashes too, so the bare receipt stays a receipt), the minute. receiptSignatureOk(publicKey, hash, text, sig, atMs) hashes the text it is handed. One function for both sides, as today: relayAuth.js is loaded by node and relay alike.
2. Every producer passes the text it sends, every verifier the text it received: peerPost 1058, 1084, 1483 and onReply; relay 2976, 3219 and routeReply.
3. deliverForwardedReply verifies first: a reply whose receipt fails against its own text is a partner error to the asker (relayErrorToAsker, 502, 'bad reply signature from partner'), no route is announced, the carrying entry goes. A reply that verifies is delivered and announced as today.

items.title: Self-addressed verbs get their own capacity (S3)
items.box:
WHAT: a request addressed to the relay itself (owner verbs, member verbs, partner searches and forwards) no longer competes for the one slot a member target gets; the relay's own verbs have capacity of their own, so one member searching cannot lock the owner out of his relay (S3 of the review, reproduced: the owner's partners and invite got 503 target is busy 100 ms after a member's search).

DECIDED: this item at Andy's word (2026-10-10, "next. same thing."). A relay-wire change: the shape is reviewed and gets his yes before any build. On Q1: "A" (2026-10-10): a route whose target is the relay itself is not counted against the per-target slot; the requester caps of 0016 and the per-minute limit are the bounds. On the caps per class (2026-10-10): the member's 1 is his Experiment 1 of 2026-10-02 (b44c3101); the relay's own class exists for device offers only, and "device WILL be KILLED. that's a decision.", so that class goes with device (its own item); the partner class's 16: his thought (2026-10-10) "that limit should theoretically be at number-of members, so the relay can reliably cover all members needs." Proposed below as B2; his reading of it: "so the partner-calls are limited to 1 per member." (2026-10-10).

CHECKED by claude-windows at b355e36d:
- router.js open() refuses with 503 'target is busy' when countForTarget(target) reaches perTarget, and perTarget is DEFAULT_PER_TARGET, which is 1 (the comment above it still says the default is max and the ceiling of 1 comes one commit later; the number is 1 today).
- relay.js 4057: a post the relay is the target of (postedToSelf, a strict match on its own key) opens its route with routes.open(selfHash, who.id, toToken, ...) where toToken is the relay's own key; so every self-addressed request of every member and partner counts against ONE target, the relay, and the second in flight is refused busy.
- Decision 0016 gives three REQUESTER budgets (member, the relay as itself, partner: caps per class, 429 'too many in flight' at router.js 312). The target ceiling is the other axis and was written for a member target: one question at a time per person. The relay as a target is not a person.
- The requester caps of 0016 are per KEY across every target: a member 1 in flight (router.js DEFAULT_PER_MEMBER), the relay acting for a member 16, a partner 16 (DEFAULT_PER_REQUESTER). So under A each member already holds exactly one slot for its self-addressed requests, which is his "1 slot per caller and/or member" (2026-10-10), without a new number.
- The rate limit (MEMBER_PER_MIN, the partner budget, relay.js 4026) already bounds how often one sender may ask the relay; the target slot adds nothing for the relay's own verbs but the lock-out.

SHAPE (proposed)
A. The plainest: a route whose target is the relay itself is not counted against the per-target ceiling at all; open() takes the target class from the kind it is already handed (routerTable.RELAY exists as a class name) or from a flag, and skips countForTarget for it. The requester caps of 0016 and the per-minute rate limit remain the bounds on self-addressed traffic; a member target keeps its one slot. No new number.
B. The alternative: a second ceiling for the relay as target (perSelf), a constant in router.js like the others, so self-addressed verbs are bounded in flight as a class. One more fixed number to justify; 0016's requester caps already bound the same traffic, so B counts the same thing twice.
Decided: A.
B2 (decided, his, 2026-10-10: "so the partner-calls are limited to 1 per member." and "which would fall under the 1 in flight per-member"): the partner class has no cap of its own; the per-target slot of one per member already bounds a partner to one in flight per member and so to the roll in all, and nothing is derived or read for it. items.title: Replay windows on the relay's signatures (S5, S8, S9)
items.box:
WHAT: three places where a signed thing can be replayed inside its time window: a sealed owner post to the relay (S5), a member's stream header on another relay (S8), and a node's own post resent unchanged on retry and after a restart past the window (S9); each gets a nonce or a tighter check so a signature serves once (the replay windows of the review).

DECIDED: an item of this goal at Andy's word (2026-10-10, "let's do it that way.": one cleanup item last and three design items, each argued one at a time before it is built). From the review of 2026-10-10 (Andreas Thut, at e8f8ffd).

CHECKED by claude-windows at b355e36d (the review's lines):
- S5: duplicates are refused only while a request is in flight (router.js 294, 389); a signature stays valid about two minutes (relayAuth.js 126); seal.open's at is never checked for self-addressed verbs (relay.js 3081); relay.js 1959 says a post cannot be replayed at all. Whoever sees a sealed owner post (the TLS terminator, a log) re-sends it: a config restart again, another invite minted, debug toggled.
- S8: the stream signature is 'stream', the key and the minute (relayAuth.js 97), naming no relay and carrying no nonce, and a new stream evicts the old one (presence.js 148); relay A replays a member's stream header on relay B within about three minutes and takes over the member's stream there.
- S9: a post is signed once (peerPost.js 908); retries and queue entries restored after a restart resend the same body; the relay accepts minutes -1, 0 and +1 only and 403 bad post signature is treated as permanent; patienceMs up to ten minutes and the persisted queue almost always end in 403.

ARGUED (2026-10-10): on S8, Andy: "isn't the stream itself already verified though the header?" (it is; the signature names no relay) and "then the header needs a signature from the relay (key)." Decided for S8: the relay's public key goes inside what the member signs for the stream header, and the relay accepts a header only when the key named is its own.

DECIDED NOT TO FIX (Andy, 2026-10-11): S5: "the way i see it, spirit-3 is my box. if the person i rent it from invades my space, they can do WAY worse that resending a dumb request. so i wouldn't fix it. same i someone has a key to my appartement, i just have to trust them. NOT worth fixing." S9: "the other issue, NOT worth fixing, we gain nothing over centralized packet distribution systems." So this item builds S8 alone: the relay's public key inside the signed stream header, the relay accepting only a header naming its own key; a post that waits past the signature window stays refused and dropped as today. The title still names S5 and S9; the rename is his.

SHAPE (as first proposed; only the S8 line is built): a nonce or the hash remembered for the window on self-addressed verbs (S5); the relay's own key in the stream message (S8); a post re-signed at send time, never at queue time (S9). All three change the wire (flag day).

FILES: relayAuth.js, relay.js, router.js, presence.js, peerPost.js (core, grant); a new suite.

Yes, the relay checks the header's signature before it opens a stream. The gap is what that signature says: only "I am this key, this minute", nothing about which relay it is for. So the same signed header opens a stream as you on any relay you are a member of, for about three minutes (the minute before and after count), and a second connect replaces the first, so whoever replays it takes your stream there. The fix for that one is the relay's own name inside what you sign, so a header made for one relay is worthless on another; the check itself stays as it is.
then the header needs a signature from the relay (key).

Yes, that is it: the relay's public key goes inside what you sign for the header, and a relay accepts a header only when the key named is its own. Recorded as decided for the stream part. Two parts of the opening question remain: a sealed request to the relay that can be re-sent for about two minutes, and a node re-sending a post signed long ago.
this green?

Not yet: the stream part is decided, two parts are not.
- A sealed request you send your relay (restart its config, mint an invite, toggle debug) can be re-sent by anyone who saw it, such as the TLS box in front of the relay, for about two minutes, and the relay does it again; fix: the relay remembers each request it has done for those two minutes and refuses a repeat.
- A node signs a post once when it queues it; a retry or a restart later re-sends that old signature past the relay's three-minute window, gets a 403, and gives up; fix: the node signs when it actually sends, every time.
Close both that way?

sure: "A sealed request you send your relay (restart its config, mint an invite, toggle debug) can be re-sent by anyone who saw it, such as the TLS box in front of the relay, for about two minutes, and the relay does it again; fix: the relay remembers each request it has done for those two minutes and refuses a repeat."

and to whom would that be useful? in what way?

Hmmm "A node signs a post once when it queues it; a retry or a restart later re-sends that old signature past the relay's three-minute window, gets a 403, and gives up; fix: the node signs when it actually sends, every time."

What difference does it make. since the node-side queues allow the relay to never store actual transmission data, and as such do the job that non-p2p central server usually do, doesn't it make sense that the signature occurs before the queuing?

On the re-sent request: useful to whoever sits between you and your relay and can see the bytes, in practice the TLS box on the relay host or a log there, and both are already trusted; what they gain is the side effect done twice (another invite minted and promised, a restart, debug flipped), and the answer itself if the relay's answer to you is not sealed, which I have not confirmed. Low value, cheap to close (a short memory of done requests); I would keep it but rank it last, or drop it at your word.
On signing before queuing: you are right that the queue is what lets the relay store nothing, and that stays exactly as it is either way; the queue holds the post in both designs. The one thing a signature carries that goes stale is the minute inside it: a post that waits more than about two minutes (relay down, a restart) arrives with an old minute, the relay refuses it, and the node treats the refusal as final and drops the post. Re-signing at the moment of sending changes nothing in the content or the queue; it only puts the current minute in. Same content, fresh stamp.
Keep both fixes, with the first ranked last?

items.title: App error codes leave the shared register (A3)
items.box:
WHAT: the shared error register, loaded by node and relay alike, defines codes that belong to apps (the desk's taken, box-moved, not-offered, no-such-item; deskClient's unblocked; chatClerver's peer-blocked; fileServer's pool-full, no-such-file, already-exists), and an app cannot define its own because define throws 'already declared'; the app codes leave the register and an app declares its codes itself (A3 of the review, rule 3: no app logic in node or relay).

DECIDED: an item of this goal at Andy's word (2026-10-10, "let's do it that way.": one cleanup item last and three design items, each argued one at a time before it is built). From the review of 2026-10-10 (Andreas Thut, at e8f8ffd).

- spiritErrors.js 731-800 defines the app codes; the comment near 802 says the register holds nothing of any app's.
- appServer.js 155 maps only the refusals it knows: remove these codes and every desk, fileServer and chatClerver refusal becomes handler-failed.
- define throws 'already declared', so an app cannot take a code over itself.

DECIDED (Andy, 2026-10-11): "yes. get the bloody app error codes out of the core." and "(i knew this was coming, and I'm glad the fix is forced now.)"; and "and make sure their codes start with \"appServerName: error text\" so the origin of the error is clear." Nothing on the wire changes (the same codes travel).
